recent_posts.title: Embracing failure leads to faster learning and growth
recent_posts.summary: A personal reflection on how fear of failure holds us back from learning and improving. Using inline skating as a central metaphor, the author argues that committing fully—even at the risk of falling—leads to faster skill development. Examples from voice lessons, saxophone, and poetry writing illustrate how embracing failure across different disciplines unlocks rapid improvement. The key insight: low-stakes failures are rarely as dangerous as the anxiety around them, and that anxiety itself causes the failures we fear.

recent_posts.title: When responsible disclosure fails and security bugs stay unfixed
recent_posts.summary: A developer describes discovering serious data leaks in prescription medication courier tracking pages — exposing customer addresses, signatures, porch photos, and even a Stripe private key. Despite multiple attempts at responsible disclosure through direct contact, pharmacy staff, and prescribers, the vulnerabilities remain unfixed due to inaccessible security contacts and unresponsive companies. The key takeaway: sometimes security issues cannot be fixed by the person who finds them, and accepting that limit is necessary after exhausting reasonable reporting options.

recent_posts.title: Binding port 0 to avoid port collisions
recent_posts.summary: Port collisions in tests—when multiple tests spin up servers and accidentally pick the same port—are a common source of flakiness. Random port selection reduces but doesn't eliminate collisions, and sequential port incrementing creates its own problems. The reliable solution is binding to port 0, which asks the OS kernel to assign a free ephemeral port from its managed range (e.g., 32768–60999 on Linux). After binding, `getsockname()` retrieves the actual assigned port so requests can be directed to it. A Rust/Tokio example demonstrates the pattern: bind a `TcpListener` to port 0, call `local_addr()` to get the assigned address, and pass it to the test client.

recent_posts.title: TIL: Docker log rotation
recent_posts.summary: Docker doesn't automatically rotate log files, which can lead to disk space issues as container logs grow indefinitely. The solution involves configuring log rotation in `/etc/docker/daemon.json` with settings like `max-size` and `max-file`, then restarting Docker and recreating containers for the changes to take effect. A 25 GB server disk was filled by Docker logs exceeding 10 GB per file due to this default behavior.

recent_posts.title: Using an engineering notebook
recent_posts.summary: Keeping a physical engineering notebook—writing detailed, dated, real-time notes by hand—can significantly improve productivity and thinking clarity. The practice involves recording work as it happens with enough detail for someone else to replicate, creating a permanent append-only record. Writing by hand aids memory retention and forces clearer thinking before coding. While only 25% of developers use this practice, it's worth experimenting with different formats and detail levels to see if it works for you.

recent_posts.title: Some good English word datasets
recent_posts.summary: WordNet and Wortschatz Leipzig frequency lists are two excellent sources for English word datasets. WordNet provides a database of word relations including definitions and synonyms, maintained as an open-source fork. Leipzig offers frequency lists from news, web, and Wikipedia sources. Unix system word lists and Wiktionary are also useful alternatives, though the former lacks clear licensing and the latter is formatted for human rather than machine consumption. These datasets are valuable for projects requiring word lists with different criteria like common words or specific subsets.

recent_posts.title: Making niche solutions is the point
recent_posts.summary: Building custom solutions tailored to specific needs is a core advantage of software engineering. Just as 3D printing enables creating niche physical objects, software development allows engineers to craft tools and applications that precisely fit their requirements. While using existing solutions saves time, the ability to design custom software—from configuration scripts to personal web apps—provides exact fits for unique problems. The key is recognizing when to build versus when to adopt existing solutions, but the real magic lies in having that choice at all.

recent_posts.title: 3D printing my laptop ergonomic setup
recent_posts.summary: A developer shares their journey designing and 3D printing a custom ergonomic laptop setup to address nerve pain and portability issues. The post details four previous iterations, their problems (weight, setup time, durability), and the design process for a new PETG-printed solution using OpenSCAD. The current version weighs 280 grams, deploys in 15 seconds, features adjustable keyboard width with locking detents, and uses dovetail joints. Future improvements include adding accessory mounts, improving rigidity, and making the design modular for different keyboards and laptops.

recent_posts.title: Bayes theorem and how we talk about medical tests
recent_posts.summary: Bayes' theorem reveals that medical test results are probabilistic, not binary. Using celiac disease testing as an example, a positive result with 93% sensitivity and 96% specificity actually means only a 19% chance of having the disease in the general population—an 80% false positive rate. The key insight is that test accuracy depends heavily on prior probability: the same positive test jumps to 72% accuracy when symptoms suggest a 10% baseline risk instead of 1%. Understanding conditional probability helps interpret what test results actually mean for individual patients.

top_posts.title: What I tell people new to on-call
top_posts.summary: Being on-call as a software engineer involves managing pressure and effectively triaging issues rather than fixing everything yourself. It's crucial to communicate frequently, call for backup when needed, keep detailed notes with timestamps, and prioritize your health. Shadowing experienced colleagues can help you learn the ropes, and remember, not all alerts are urgent. Try to enjoy the process and find joy in resolving issues as a team.

top_posts.title: Rust needs a web framework for lazy developers
top_posts.summary: Rust lacks a comprehensive web framework similar to Django, making it challenging for developers to create web applications with minimal effort. The author argues for the need of a Rust web framework that includes essential features like routing, templating, static file serving, logins, permissions, database interface, and admin tooling, among others. Existing Rust frameworks either focus on minimalism or single-page apps, requiring extensive manual setup. A new web toolkit called 'nicole's web toolkit' is proposed to streamline development with pre-configured tools and features.

top_posts.title: Abusing Talon to use my eye tracker in a project
top_posts.summary: The author describes how they used Talon, a voice-control software, to integrate an eye tracker into a project. They discuss challenges with using the Tobii 5 eye tracker on Linux, as its native SDK supports only more expensive models and is Windows-based. They detail creating a Python script to use Talon's eye tracker module, handling gaze data, and setting up a hot-reloading server to expose this data. Despite some integration hurdles, they successfully linked the eye tracker to a Rust program, enabling eye-tracking inputs for a game development project.
